name: highest-points-of-europe

description.en: The highest point of 40 sovereign states of Europe, one card each: the states that the UN's M49 standard places in Europe, Russia included and Cyprus, Turkey and the Caucasus states not, leaving out Italy, Serbia, Monaco and Vatican City, whose highest point is disputed or not a named summit. Front: the country, e.g. “Highest point of Sweden”; back: the name of the summit in English and Swedish, often with a short note. For Denmark the card asks about Denmark proper (without Greenland and the Faroe Islands), for the Netherlands about the European part. Taken from Wikidata and checked against the CIA World Factbook's last edition, Wikipedia and national sources.
description.sv: Den högsta punkten i 40 självständiga stater i Europa, ett kort för varje: de stater som FN:s standard M49 räknar till Europa, med Ryssland men utan Cypern, Turkiet och Kaukasusländerna, och utan Italien, Serbien, Monaco och Vatikanstaten, vars högsta punkt är omstridd eller inte en namngiven topp. Framsida: landet, t.ex. ”Högsta punkten i Sverige”; baksida: toppens namn på engelska och svenska, ofta med en kort anteckning. För Danmark gäller kortet det egentliga Danmark (utan Grönland och Färöarna), för Nederländerna den europeiska delen. Uppgifterna är hämtade från Wikidata och kontrollerade mot den sista utgåvan av CIA:s World Factbook, Wikipedia och nationella källor.

method: Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.

1. Wikidata (query 1): every item that is a sovereign state (P31 Q3624078) on the continent Europe (P30 Q46), apart from states with limited recognition (P31 Q3024240), with its M49 code (P2082), every P610 (highest point) statement with its rank, the English, Swedish and mul labels of the point and its elevation (P2044). The result has 49 items, among them the transcontinental Russia, Turkey, Georgia and Kazakhstan and Cyprus (Armenia and Azerbaijan are not on the continent Europe in Wikidata), but neither Denmark (Q35) nor the Netherlands (Q55), whose items are constituent countries; their P610 statements were fetched with query 2. Query 1 also returned the items Kingdom of Denmark and Kingdom of the Netherlands and, despite the filter, Kosovo; none of the three is a card.

2. Selection: the states were limited to those that the UN Statistics Division's M49 standard places in its region Europe (code 150), parsed from the M49 overview page (query 5, script m49.py: the rows of the page's first, English table whose third cell, Region Code, is "150"): 51 rows, of which 44 are sovereign states (43 UN members and the Holy See) and 7 are dependencies (Åland, the Faroe Islands, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Jersey, Svalbard and Jan Mayen, Gibraltar). So M49 decides which states get a card (see Licensing for why that is a fact that may be used). An attempt to corroborate the region membership from Wikidata (query 16: states that are part of (P361) the items with the M49 codes 154, 151, 039 and 155) returned no rows, because Wikidata does not link the states to those items. M49 puts Russia in Eastern Europe, and Cyprus, Turkey, Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan in Western Asia and Kazakhstan in Central Asia, so those six are not in the deck, and Russia's card asks for the highest point of Russia as a whole (Mount Elbrus, in the Caucasus). Four of the 44 were then left out (see Selection): Italy, Serbia, Monaco and Vatican City. 40 cards.

3. Independent check, all states: The World Factbook of the CIA, discontinued in February 2026, was read in its last edition from the public-domain factbook.json repository (query 6; country files last updated 22 January 2026), field Geography > Elevation > highest point. Further check: the English Wikipedia's "List of highest points of European countries" (revision 1374673390), fetched as wikitext through the MediaWiki API and parsed by enwiki_parse.py (query 7). Every card's summit was compared with both by reading the three readings side by side; the differences are listed under quality control (round 0).

4. National and other sources where the readings differed or a fact changes: for Sweden the Tarfala research station's 2026 measurement of Kebnekaise (11 September 2026) as published by Stockholm University on 16 September 2026 (query 9; the dossier first cited the 2025 measurement, see quality-control round 1); for Luxembourg the national statistics office's "Luxembourg in figures 2025" (query 10) and the English Wikipedia article Kneiff (query 8); for Denmark the Lex (Den Store Danske) article Møllehøj (query 11). The brief named Lantmäteriet; Stockholm University's Tarfala station makes the annual measurement of the Kebnekaise peaks, so its report was used instead.

5. Names: the English back is the Wikidata English label of the summit, except for Belarus, where the English label "Dziaržynkaja hara" is a Belarusian Latin form that no other source uses: the card uses the English alias "Dzyarzhynskaya Hara" (also the Factbook's and the English Wikipedia's form). The Swedish back is the Wikidata Swedish label where it equals the title of the Swedish Wikipedia article (sitelink, query 3) and the local official form; otherwise: Ireland "Carrauntoohil" (the Irish official form and a Swedish alias; the Swedish label is "Carrauntoohill" and the Swedish article "Carrantuohill"), Finland "Haldefjäll" (the Swedish Wikipedia title and Finland-Swedish name, also an English alias; the Swedish label writes "Halde fjäll"; changed from "Halti" in quality-control round 2), Malta "Ta' Dmejrek" (the mul label, with the Maltese apostrophe and space; the Swedish label is "Ta'Dmejrek"), Croatia "Dinara" (the mul label; there is no Swedish label or article). Where Swedish and English differ the Swedish form is the one in Swedish use (Olympos, Elbrus, Moldoveanu, Aukštojas, Dealul Bălănești, Ponta do Pico, Hvannadalshnjúkur, Gora Dzerzjinskaja). Liechtenstein's card says "Vorder-Grauspitz" in both languages (the Swedish label and article, the Factbook and the English list; the English label is "Grauspitz"), so the answer does not depend on the language (quality-control round 2). Country names are the Wikidata English and Swedish labels, with "Czechia" (the short name the UN uses, an English alias) for the Czech Republic. Swedish fronts read "Högsta punkten i <land>", which avoids genitives of names such as Schweiz, except for the island states, where Swedish says "på": "Högsta punkten på Island" and "Högsta punkten på Malta". English fronts read "Highest point of <country>", with the article where English uses one ("the United Kingdom", "the European Netherlands").

6. Swedish check: the introductions of the Swedish Wikipedia articles were fetched through the MediaWiki API with their revision ids (query 4, svwiki.py); the evidence quotes the sentences of the introduction (split at ". ") that contain a keyword chosen per card: "högsta" for most cards ("högst" for Iceland), plus or instead: Andorra "Coma Pedrosa är", Belgium "ås", Bosnia and Herzegovina "gränsen" and "Veliki", Czechia "Tjeckiens" and "gränsen", Finland "Finlands" and "Norge", France "Alpernas", Germany "Österrike", the Netherlands "trelandsgränspunkt", Poland "gränsen" and "Slovakien", Romania "Făgăraș", Russia "Elbrus (" and "Europas", Slovakia "Karpaterna", Spain "Spaniens" and "Teneriffa", Sweden "Nordtoppen", Switzerland "Monte Rosa", Ukraine "Hoverla (" and the United Kingdom "Skottland"; if none matched, the first sentence (Zla Kolata, whose introduction does not call it Montenegro's highest point). Dinara has no Swedish article. Germany's sentence on the Bavarian Alps was added to the evidence by hand in quality-control round 3.

7. Cards: front "Highest point of <country>" / "Högsta punkten i <land>" ("på" for Iceland and Malta); back: the summit; backNote: short context (mountain range, border, the mainland high point of Spain and Portugal, other names), every fact of it from one of the sources named in the card's evidence. Elevations are left off the cards because surveys differ; the one exception is Kebnekaise's north peak, given with its source and year because the change of Sweden's highest point is the point of the note. Denmark and the Netherlands are asked about their European part: Denmark proper (front note), whose highest point is Møllehøj (the Kingdom of Denmark's is Gunnbjørn Fjeld in Greenland), and the European Netherlands, whose highest point is the Vaalserberg (the whole country's is Mount Scenery on Saba). Study direction front to back, because Korab answers two cards (Albania and North Macedonia).

8. The dossier was generated from the saved query results by make_dossier.py, which writes each card's evidence from the parsed readings (the Wikidata statements and labels, the Factbook text, the English Wikipedia row, the Swedish Wikipedia sentence); the Stockholm University, STATEC, Kneiff and Lex readings were added by hand from the fetched pages, and the changes of quality-control rounds 1–3 were made by hand from the readings of queries 9 and 13–16. The scripts are not published with the deck; the steps above give what they do, including the parsing rule of m49.py (step 2) and the keywords of svwiki.py's sentence choice (step 6).

9. Machine checks: for every card the builder checks against live Wikidata that the country item has the summit as a P610 value, that the summit has the English and Swedish back as a label or alias (in that language or mul), and that the country item has the English and Swedish country name of the front. For the Netherlands the builder's P610 check cannot be used: it reads only best-rank values, and the Vaalserberg is a normal-rank P610 value of Q55 beside the preferred Mount Scenery (query 2), so the card checks instead that the Vaalserberg's country (P17) is the Netherlands. That is only a sanity check (the Vaalserberg also has Belgium and Germany as P17 values); the real Wikidata support for the card is the normal-rank P610 value of Q55 read with query 2. Two label checks are left out on purpose: Finland's Swedish back "Haldefjäll" is the Swedish Wikipedia sitelink of Q216035 but not a Swedish label or alias (the label is "Halde fjäll"), and Liechtenstein's English back "Vorder-Grauspitz" is not an English label or alias of Q665000 (the label is "Grauspitz"); both are documented in the cards' evidence. The built deck was validated with the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators (validate_sources.ts).
selection: The sovereign states that the UN M49 standard places in Europe (43 UN members and the Holy See), as of 4 October 2026, each with its highest point: 40 cards. Transcontinental states follow M49: Russia is in (its highest point is Mount Elbrus in the Caucasus, the highest point of Russia as a whole), while Turkey, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Cyprus (Western Asia) and Kazakhstan (Central Asia) are out; so are Kosovo (not a UN member and not listed by M49) and the dependencies (Åland, the Faroe Islands, Gibraltar, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Jersey, Svalbard and Jan Mayen). Left out of the 44: Italy, because sources differ on whether its highest point is Mont Blanc or the Mont Blanc de Courmayeur (French and Italian maps disagree about the border at the summit; Wikidata gives Mont Blanc, the Factbook the Mont Blanc de Courmayeur); Serbia, because its highest point depends on whether Kosovo is counted (Wikidata's normal-rank value is Velika Rudoka in Kosovo, the Factbook gives Midžor); Monaco, whose highest point is a spot on the road Chemin des Révoires on the slope of Mont Agel, not a summit; and Vatican City, whose highest point is an unnamed spot in the Vatican Gardens on the Vatican Hill. For Denmark and the Netherlands, whose highest points overall lie outside Europe (Greenland, Saba), the cards ask for the European part; Spain's and Portugal's cards keep the country as a whole (Teide on Tenerife, Mount Pico in the Azores) and name the mainland high point in the note, as all the sources do.

licensing: The only content source is Wikidata, whose structured data is CC0: which summit is each state's highest point, the English and Swedish names of the summits and states and the alternative names in the notes come from it, so the deck is CC0 1.0 like the rest of the library. Every other source was used for verification only: the CIA World Factbook (public domain, but not needed as content), the English and Swedish Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0), the UN M49 page (UN terms of use, non-commercial), Stockholm University, STATEC and Lex (all rights reserved or no open licence). They confirmed facts, and no wording or table was copied from them; the fronts and notes are the compiler's own wording of facts. The one thing a verification source decided is which states get a card: the deck follows the UN M49 standard's region Europe. M49 is a classification that assigns every country or area of the world to one region; that a state belongs to its region Europe is a fact of the standard, as an ISO code is, and facts are not protected by copyright, so using them to decide the deck's scope copies nothing protected. No list was taken over: the deck's items are the states with their Wikidata highest points, with exclusions decided and explained here, and the English Wikipedia list's own selection, which differs, was not used.

rounds.lens: Sources, licences and machine checks: every card's summit against Wikidata P610, the Factbook's last edition and the English Wikipedia list; the Swedish names against Wikidata sv labels and the Swedish Wikipedia; national sources where these differed.

rounds.summary: Wikidata, the Factbook and the English Wikipedia name the same summit for 38 of the 40 states (the Factbook still names Kebnekaise's south peak). The two differences (Luxembourg, the Netherlands) were settled with a national source or by restricting the question; two states whose highest point differs by source (Italy, Serbia) and two without a named summit (Monaco, Vatican City) were left out.
